summary:
Misssion Umbral is a 2D educational game about lunar mission planning and sample extraction, built using real slope data from NASA’s Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LRO-LOLA) at the Moon’s South Pole, covering Shackleton Crater Rim, Connecting Ridge, and de Gerlache Crater Rim.

Before liftoff, players step into the role of mission engineers to evaluate routes, weigh payload mass in kilograms, and balance battery energy in watt-hours, following the real trade-study approach of NASA Goddard’s Mission Design Lab and VIPER lunar operations. After making a mid-flight descent decision, players explore the lunar surface, collect samples across steep terrain, and calculate whether they have enough power to make it back to the lander.

By turning raw orbital topography into playable engineering decisions, Misión Umbral helps anyone experience how terrain slope and resource limits shape real space exploration.
details:
What It Does and How It Works

Mission Umbral is a 2D lunar mission and extraction game powered by real elevation data from NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter LOLA. Players plan and execute a complete lunar south pole mission across three landing sites: Shackleton Crater Rim, Connecting Ridge, and de Gerlache Crater Rim.

1. Mission Design: Drawing from NASA Goddard's Mission Design Lab workflow, players evaluate routes, balance payload weight in kilograms against battery power in watt-hours, and configure their equipment before launch.

2. Trajectory Choice: During descent, players decide whether to burn extra fuel for a precise landing or save fuel and face a longer surface drive.

3. Surface Operations: Players drive the rover across real terrain to drill and collect samples, keeping a constant eye on return energy before heading back to the lander.

Use of NASA Data and Engineering Factors

We processed 5-meter-per-pixel GeoTIFF slope files from the NASA Goddard Planetary Geodynamics Data Archive, covering Site04 for Shackleton, Site01 for Connecting Ridge, and Site11 for de Gerlache. Every pixel represents real terrain slope, directly driving movement friction and power drain. While the altimetry data comes straight from NASA, energy physics and mission scoring are simulated using NASA VIPER operations as a baseline.

Benefits and Intended Impact

Space engineering often looks abstract on paper. Misión Umbral turns raw orbital data into immediate physical consequences, letting anyone experience why steep slopes drain batteries, why payload weight matters, and why safety margins keep a mission alive.

Creativity and Development Tools

Instead of using static artwork, real NASA elevation grids dictate gameplay physics and route selection. The project was built using web technologies, Visual Studio Code, Git, Python for geospatial data conversion, and AI tools for rapid coding support.
